clinicalPearls: A distensible venous malformation of the orbit that enlarges with raised venous pressure
The hallmark is positional or Valsalva-induced proptosis, appearing or worsening on bending, straining or the Valsalva manoeuvre
It may be asymptomatic or cause intermittent proptosis, pain and, occasionally, acute thrombosis or haemorrhage
Imaging with the patient performing Valsalva, or in a dependent position, demonstrates the distending lesion
Enophthalmos can occur when the varix is decompressed and the orbit is at rest
Many are observed, with intervention reserved for significant symptoms, thrombosis or visual compromise
reference.pathophysiology: An orbital varix is a low-flow venous malformation consisting of dilated, thin-walled venous channels that communicate with the orbital venous system. Because these channels distend under increased venous pressure, manoeuvres that raise it (bending forward, straining, Valsalva) cause the varix to fill and produce proptosis, which reverses at rest. Stagnation within the malformation predisposes to thrombosis, and thin vessel walls can bleed, causing acute pain and proptosis; chronic changes may leave enophthalmos from orbital fat atrophy.
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI with and without Valsalva or in a dependent position
Imaging to detect phleboliths and to exclude a fistula
Evaluation of optic nerve function if compromise is suspected
Vascular imaging where a high-flow lesion must be excluded
redFlags: Acute painful proptosis suggesting thrombosis or haemorrhage
Optic nerve compromise with visual loss
Features suggesting a high-flow vascular lesion
reference.prognosis: Most orbital varices are benign and can be observed; complications such as thrombosis or haemorrhage are usually self-limiting, and intervention for symptomatic lesions carries a risk of significant bleeding.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by imaging only at rest without a distending manoeuvre
Confusing it with a lymphatic malformation or a fistula
Overlooking acute thrombosis or haemorrhage as a cause of sudden proptosis
Underestimating the bleeding risk of surgical intervention
management: Observe asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic lesions, which is the mainstay of care
Reserve intervention for significant symptoms, recurrent thrombosis, disfiguring proptosis or visual compromise, using surgical excision or endovascular embolisation and sclerotherapy
Provide supportive management with analgesia for acute thrombosis or haemorrhage, which is usually self-limiting
Monitor optic nerve function and vision when compression is a concern
Characterise and follow the lesion with Valsalva or dependent-position imaging, excluding a high-flow vascular malformation
Refer to oculoplastic and interventional or vascular specialists for treatment planning
